title: It seemed right to him
hookLine: when someone wrongs you, remember he did what seemed right to him (Enchiridion 42)

lines: A WHOLE STORY IN HALF A SECOND.
cards: Someone cuts you off in traffic, and in the half second before the horn, a whole story forms in your head about who they are. Selfish. Reckless.
Probably like this all the time. Hardly anyone pauses to tell the other story: that from inside that car, the move made sense. Late for a shift.
A kid crying in the back. A misjudged mirror. Or simply a belief that the lane was theirs.
Section forty-two of the handbook asks you to tell that second story, every time.

teach.h: HE DID WHAT SEEMED RIGHT TO HIM.
teach.b: When someone treats you badly or speaks badly of you, Epictetus says, remember that he does it or says it because he thinks it's right for him to. He can't act on what seems right to you. Only on what seems right to him.

teach.h: THE ONE DECEIVED IS THE ONE HARMED.
teach.b: If what seemed right to him is wrong, he's the one harmed, because he's the one who was deceived. Epictetus gives an example from logic: if someone takes a true statement to be false, the statement isn't harmed.
The person who got it wrong is.
The root is an idea often traced to Socrates, in Plato's dialogues: that nobody does wrong knowingly, believing it to be wrong. People act on what looks good to them, even when it isn't.
The Stoics inherited that idea and built on it. So the person who wrongs you isn't a monster who chose evil. They're someone who saw it wrong.
From here, Epictetus says, you'll be gentle with the one who insults you.

teach.h: SAY IT EACH TIME: IT SEEMED SO TO HIM.
teach.b: And he gives a short phrase to say each time, only two words in his Greek, a little like a breath before reacting: it seemed so to him. That isn't an excuse for harm.
You can still protect yourself, set a limit, even seek justice.
What changes is the heat. You stop adding your own anger to their mistake. You see a person who judged badly, not an enemy.
And that turns out to be lighter to carry.

how: People practicing Stoicism often remind themselves, when wronged, that the other person acted on what seemed right to them, which helps them respond without adding anger.

o: the Stoic who wrote down the handbook's sayings
a Roman emperor who kept a Stoic notebook
the thinker behind 'nobody does wrong knowingly'

games.q: it seemed right to him — tap the pairs.
p: doing what seemed right to him
a true statement taken as false
the person is harmed, not it

s: Epictetus says the person who wrongs you is the one harmed, if they judged wrongly
the one deceived is the one hurt, like someone who mistakes a true statement for false.
this teaching means putting up with any harm done to you
it changes the heat, not your right to set limits or seek justice.

games.q: a coworker takes credit for your idea in a meeting. what phrase does Epictetus offer?
games.why: he did what seemed right to him. if he judged wrongly, he's the one harmed. that frees you to respond without adding anger.

practice: Bring to mind someone who wronged you, not the worst, just someone: a sharp email, a broken promise, a rude driver.
For a minute, stand where they stood and ask what they believed was true, or fair, or necessary; you don't have to agree, just look.
Then say quietly, it seemed right to him, or to her, or to them, and notice what happens to the heat.

wordCard.voice: Socrates. The thinker behind the idea that nobody does wrong knowingly; anyone who wrongs you acted on what seemed right to them, and their mistake is their harm. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: it seemed so to him, the two Greek words Enchiridion 42 asks you to say each time.

carryVoice: Your line: lighter to carry. Two words can cool a lot of heat. That's day three hundred seventy-seven.

sources.ref: Plato, Protagoras 345d–e, 358c–d (no one does wrong willingly)
